clinicalPearls: Caused by recessive variants in SGCB encoding beta-sarcoglycan, one of the four sarcoglycanopathies (LGMD R3-R6).
The phenotype is frequently more severe than alpha-sarcoglycanopathy, with earlier onset and a higher likelihood of significant cardiac involvement.
Dilated cardiomyopathy is a well-recognised and sometimes early complication, so cardiac surveillance should not wait for advanced limb weakness.
Presentation resembles Duchenne muscular dystrophy with proximal weakness, calf hypertrophy, Gowers sign and greatly elevated creatine kinase.
Beta-sarcoglycan is considered a core scaffold of the sarcoglycan complex, so its loss tends to destabilise the whole tetramer strongly on immunostaining.
Respiratory muscle weakness commonly accompanies cardiac disease and both contribute to long-term morbidity.
Intellect is normal, helping distinguish it from dystrophinopathy despite the shared motor pattern.
reference.pathophysiology: LGMD R4 is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in SGCB on chromosome 4q12, encoding beta-sarcoglycan. Beta-sarcoglycan is a central structural component of the sarcoglycan subcomplex within the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex and is thought to act as a scaffold around which alpha, gamma and delta assemble at the sarcolemma. Pathogenic changes in beta-sarcoglycan therefore tend to cause profound loss of the entire complex, severing the mechanical bridge between the cytoskeleton and the basal lamina. Myofibre membranes are consequently prone to contraction-induced injury, driving repeated necrosis-regeneration cycles, inflammation and fibrosis in skeletal muscle. Because the same complex is expressed in cardiac muscle and vascular smooth muscle, its disruption also predisposes to dilated cardiomyopathy, which is a more consistent and sometimes early feature of the beta- and delta-subtypes than of the alpha-subtype.
additionalDifferentials: Delta-sarcoglycanopathy / LGMD R6 (SGCD), which shares prominent cardiomyopathy
Other genetic causes of childhood dilated cardiomyopathy with myopathy
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography and electrocardiography at diagnosis with regular follow-up, plus cardiac MRI where available
Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry for the sarcoglycan complex and dystrophin
Targeted SGCB sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis or an LGMD gene panel
Pulmonary function testing including supine spirometry
redFlags: Symptoms of heart failure such as breathlessness, orthopnoea or oedema, or arrhythmia
Early loss of ambulation suggesting a severe phenotype
Nocturnal hypoventilation with morning headache and disturbed sleep
Falling ventricular function on surveillance imaging
reference.prognosis: Beta-sarcoglycanopathy is often among the more severe sarcoglycanopathies, with earlier loss of ambulation in severe cases. Prognosis is heavily influenced by the frequently prominent dilated cardiomyopathy and by respiratory muscle involvement, both of which require proactive surveillance.
pitfalls: Deferring cardiac assessment until limb weakness is advanced, missing early dilated cardiomyopathy
Attributing the picture to dystrophinopathy without genetic confirmation
Assuming all sarcoglycanopathies behave like the milder alpha-subtype
Missing arrhythmia risk that can be independent of the degree of skeletal weakness
references: Peer-reviewed limb-girdle muscular dystrophy classification and consensus statements
management: No disease-modifying drug therapy exists; management is supportive within a specialist neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Proactive lifelong cardiac surveillance for the frequently prominent dilated cardiomyopathy using echocardiography, ECG and cardiac MRI, not deferring until limb weakness is advanced

Treat established cardiomyopathy with standard heart-failure therapy such as ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, beta-blockers and aldosterone antagonists, with device therapy where indicated
Respiratory surveillance including supine spirometry, with non-invasive ventilation for hypoventilation
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy for contracture prevention, orthoses and mobility aids, plus orthopaedic and spinal monitoring for scoliosis
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
Escalate to advanced heart-failure care with transplant assessment and to ventilatory support as cardiac or respiratory failure progresses
